## Where we got to

Yesterday you built, from scratch:

- an **SIR model**, derived from its assumptions rather than quoted
- the same model as a **discrete-time** recursion
- $R_0$, the epidemic threshold, the peak, the final size
- a working Julia toolchain: REPL, environments, VS Code, Quarto

That is a real day's work, and none of it needed Julia.

::: {.notes}
Open by conceding the point rather than defending it. Everything yesterday could
have been done in R, Python or MATLAB, and most of the room has done exactly that
before. Say so plainly — it buys credibility for the rest of the session.
:::

## An honest accounting

We made five claims for Julia yesterday. We **demonstrated none of them**.

| We said | You actually saw |
|---|---|
| Julia is fast | one ODE solved in milliseconds |
| Multiple dispatch makes code modular | `solve` called on one problem type |
| Macros let you rewrite code | the word "macro" |
| Automatic differentiation is built in | nothing |
| The modelling ecosystem is rich | one solver and a `for` loop |

::: {.notes}
Put this table up and leave it up. Read the right-hand column aloud; it is
deliberately unflattering. Anyone who came in sceptical is currently correct, and
naming that is more persuasive than another round of assertion.

Today is not more claims. Each row gets paid off by a specific session, and by
this evening you can check the receipts.
:::

## Claim 1 — "Julia is fast"

Yesterday: one ODE, solved faster than you could notice. So what?

Speed only matters when you need the **same model run thousands of times**:

- **Session 1** — stochastic jump processes. One realisation tells you nothing;
  you need hundreds to see a distribution.
- **Session 3** — a parameter sweep over a Latin hypercube design, hundreds of
  solves, then sensitivity indices on top.

The question is not "is one solve fast" but "can you afford the study you
actually want".

::: {.notes}
This is the honest version of the speed argument. Benchmarks of a single ODE
solve are close to meaningless — every language solves a three-compartment model
instantly. What changes the science is whether an ensemble of a thousand runs is
a coffee break or an overnight job, because that determines which questions you
are willing to ask.
:::

## Claim 2 — "Multiple dispatch makes code modular"

Yesterday you called `solve` exactly once, on an `ODEProblem`.

Today the same verb takes entirely different mathematics:

```julia
solve(ODEProblem(...),  Tsit5())        # deterministic, continuous
solve(SDEProblem(...),  LambaEM())      # stochastic, continuous
solve(JumpProblem(...), SSAStepper())   # stochastic, discrete events
```

Same function, same mental model, three different kinds of process — and none of
these were written to know about the others.

::: {.notes}
The payoff is not that it looks tidy. It is that what you learn about the solver
interface transfers: saveat, callbacks, tolerances, ensembles all behave the same
way across problem types you have never used.

Sessions 1 and 2 use all three of these, and session 4 adds an optimisation
problem to the list.
:::

## Claim 3 — "Macros let you rewrite code"

Yesterday: the word, and nothing behind it.

Today you write the *model* rather than its equations:

```julia
sir = @reaction_network begin
    κ, S + I --> 2I
    γ, I --> R
end
```

Two lines of chemistry. The macro turns them into whichever system you ask for.

::: {.notes}
Worth being precise about what a macro is doing here: it is reading that block as
syntax, before anything runs, and generating the stoichiometry and rate laws from
it. You are not calling a function that parses a string — the code itself is the
input.

Session 2. Point out that this is also the moment the model stops being a
right-hand-side function you hand-differentiate and starts being an object other
tools can analyse.
:::

## Claim 4 — "Automatic differentiation is built in"

Yesterday: mentioned, never used.

Today, in session 3: how sensitive is the epidemic peak to each parameter?

- Not a finite difference, with a step size to agonise over
- The **variational equations**, solved alongside the model
- Exact derivatives, to solver tolerance

The same machinery underlies fitting models to data, which is where most of you
will meet it again.

::: {.notes}
If anyone has spent an afternoon tuning a finite-difference step, this is the
slide that lands. Too large and you measure curvature, too small and you measure
floating-point noise; autodiff removes the dial entirely.

Session 3 also shows where the derivative stops being enough, which is the more
interesting half of the story.
:::

## Claim 5 — "The ecosystem is rich"

Yesterday: a solver and a `for` loop. Available anywhere.

Today, from that *same* two-line network:

- an **ODE** system, an **SDE** system, a **jump** process — no rewriting
- equations for the **mean and variance** directly, without simulating
- the **full probability distribution** over states, including the chance the
  outbreak dies out

::: {.notes}
This is the claim that is hardest to demonstrate and most worth demonstrating,
because it is not about any one package. It is that the packages compose: Catalyst
hands its network to the solvers, to MomentClosure, and to the finite state
projection, none of which were written with the others in mind.

The extinction probability is the one to dwell on. No amount of ODE work gives it
to you, and it is exactly the quantity a public health question often turns on.
:::

## The parallel machine you already have

Most of us do not have a cluster.

- A local server or a cloud account is a procurement problem, a queueing system
  and somebody to administer it.
- The laptop in front of you has **4 to 12 cores**, and they are idle.
- Yesterday, every model you ran used one of them.

Today's ensembles are the easy case — 200 independent epidemics that share
nothing:

```julia
solve(ensemble, SSAStepper(), EnsembleThreads(); trajectories = 200)
```

::: {.notes}
Ask for a show of hands: who has access to a compute cluster? Usually a couple
of people. Then ask who has at least four cores in the machine they are working
on. Almost everyone. That gap is the point of this slide.

Stochastic epidemic modelling is unusually well suited to this, because
replicate simulations are independent by construction. There is no
communication to arrange and no partial results to combine — the hard part of
parallel programming simply is not present.
:::

## Threads, and the one thing to do first

| | shared-memory threading |
|---|---|
| **Julia** | built in: `Threads.@threads`, `EnsembleThreads()` |
| **Python** | the GIL stops threads helping CPU-bound work; you reach for processes, and copy data between them |
| **R** | no threading in the language; fork or socket workers, and copy data |

You must choose the number of threads **before Julia starts**:

```bash
export JULIA_NUM_THREADS=auto     # or julia --threads=auto
```

In VS Code, set `julia.NumThreads`. Then check:

```julia
Threads.nthreads()     # if this says 1, EnsembleThreads() buys you nothing
```

::: {.notes}
Be fair to the other languages rather than scoring a point. Python and R can
both use every core on the machine; what they cannot easily do is share memory
while doing it, so you end up copying the model and the data into each worker
process. For a big model or a big dataset that copy is the expensive part, and
it is why parallel code in those languages so often runs slower than the serial
version until it is tuned.

The last line is the one that actually costs people time today. The thread count
is fixed when the process starts, so it cannot be changed from inside a running
session, and the default is one. Nothing errors and nothing warns:
`EnsembleThreads()` on a single-threaded session simply runs the trajectories one
after another. If somebody reports that threading "did nothing", this is almost
always why — have them run `Threads.nthreads()` first.
:::

## Today, and which promise it pays

| Session | Topic | Pays off |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Jump processes | speed, dispatch, threads |
| 2 | Reaction networks and moment closure | macros, ecosystem, dispatch |
| 3 | Sensitivity and identifiability | autodiff, speed |
| 4 | Interventions and optimization | dispatch, ecosystem |

::: {.notes}
Keep this short — it is a map, not a lecture. The one thing to say aloud is that
sessions 2 and 3 are the crux: session 2 is where one specification turns into
five different models, and session 3 is where you find out that two of the
parameters cannot be told apart no matter how good your data is.
:::

## The thing to watch for

By this evening, ask yourself of each session:

> Could I have done that as easily in the language I came here using?

For yesterday, the honest answer is **yes**.

If it is still yes tonight, Julia has not earned its place in your work — and
that is a perfectly reasonable conclusion to reach.

::: {.notes}
End on this rather than a sales pitch. Inviting the negative verdict is what makes
the positive one worth anything, and it also sets the right standard: a tool
earns its keep by enabling work you would not otherwise attempt, not by being
pleasant.

Then go straight into session 1.
:::
